title: Unit Testing Principles
summary: What separates a unit test that's actually worth keeping from one that just adds noise — a single responsibility, real isolation, and a name that explains the failure on its own.

slides.markdown:
Not every test that compiles and passes is a good test. A unit test earns its keep by doing exactly one job: proving **one behavior** works, and failing for **one reason** when it doesn't.

That sounds obvious until you've read a test file where a single test method sets up three objects, calls four methods, and asserts ten different things — and then fails, and nobody can tell from the failure alone which of the ten things actually broke.

This topic covers the structural habits (AAA, FIRST, isolation, naming) that keep individual unit tests small, fast, and honest — the raw material the rest of this group builds on.

slides.sectionTitle: One behavior, one reason to fail
slides.markdown:
The defining property of a good unit test: when it fails, you should be able to tell **what broke** without reading the test's internals, just from its name and the assertion message.

This is a stronger requirement than "tests one function." A single function can have many behaviors — a `withdraw()` method behaves differently for a valid amount, a negative amount, and an amount exceeding the balance. Each of those is a separate behavior and deserves its own test, even though they all call the same function.

The test-per-behavior discipline is what makes a red test suite actionable instead of a puzzle. A failing test named `withdraw_rejectsNegativeAmount` tells you exactly where to look; a failing test named `testWithdraw` that exercises five scenarios tells you nothing until you open it and read every line.

AAA is the structural template almost every readable unit test follows, in three visually separated sections:

```python
def test_withdraw_rejects_amount_exceeding_balance():
    # Arrange
    account = Account(balance=100)

    # Act
    result = account.withdraw(150)

    # Assert
    assert result.is_error
    assert account.balance == 100
```

- **Arrange** builds the exact state the test needs — no more, no less.
- **Act** performs the single action under test, ideally one line.
- **Assert** checks the outcome.

The value isn't ceremony — it's that a test violating this shape (assertions scattered between actions, multiple acts) is usually a sign the test is checking more than one behavior. If you can't cleanly draw the three sections, that's a signal to split the test.

slides.subTitle: Fast, Isolated, Repeatable, Self-checking, Timely
slides.markdown:
FIRST is a checklist for whether a test deserves to be called a *unit* test at all:

- **Fast** — milliseconds, not seconds. A suite people avoid running isn't providing feedback.
- **Isolated** — no dependency on other tests' order or leftover state; each test sets up everything it needs.
- **Repeatable** — same result every time, in any environment — no reliance on system clock, network, or random seeds without control.
- **Self-checking** — the test itself reports pass/fail; no human has to eyeball console output to decide.
- **Timely** — written close to when the production code is written, not weeks later as an afterthought (or never).

A test that opens a real network connection violates Fast and Repeatable simultaneously. A test that depends on a previous test having run first violates Isolated. Any one violation degrades the whole suite's trustworthiness, because a slow or flaky test trains people to ignore red builds.

Isolation means a test's outcome depends only on what it set up, never on what another test did before it or the order tests happen to run in.

The usual culprit is shared mutable state: a module-level list, a static counter, a database row created by a previous test and never cleaned up. Two tests that individually pass can fail together — or worse, fail only when run in one specific order, which is exactly the kind of bug that passes locally and fails in CI (or vice versa) for no discoverable reason.

The fix is mechanical: each test creates its own fixtures from scratch (a fresh object, a fresh in-memory list, a transaction rolled back at teardown) rather than reusing anything another test touched. If your test suite can't be run with tests in random order and still pass, isolation is broken somewhere.

The single biggest fork in unit-testing style: do you assert on **what the code produces** (outputs, observable state, calls to true collaborators) or **how it produces it** (private methods, internal call order, internal fields)?

| | Testing behavior | Testing implementation |
|---|---|---|
| What it asserts | public inputs/outputs, observable side effects | internal structure, private state, call sequence |
| Survives refactoring | yes, as long as behavior is unchanged | no — breaks on any internal reshuffle |
| Coupling | to the contract | to the current code shape |

Testing implementation details produces tests that break every time you refactor, even when you haven't changed what the code *does* — which trains developers to fear refactoring or to skip updating tests honestly. Testing behavior means a test only turns red when something a user or caller would actually notice has changed.

The practical rule: if writing the test requires reaching into a private method or field, that's usually the test grabbing implementation instead of behavior.

A test name is the first — and sometimes only — thing a developer reads when a build goes red. `testWithdraw2` tells you nothing; `withdraw_rejectsAmountExceedingBalance_andLeavesBalanceUnchanged` tells you exactly what broke before you open the file.

A reliable pattern: **`<unit under test>_<scenario>_<expected outcome>`**. It reads almost like a sentence: "when you withdraw an amount exceeding the balance, it's rejected and the balance is unchanged."

This matters more than it sounds like it should, because in a CI failure list with forty red tests, good names let you triage in seconds — which ones are the same root cause, which are unrelated, which are the one you actually need to open. A test suite with uniformly vague names (`test1`, `testEdgeCase`) turns every red build into an investigation.

slides.sectionTitle: Brittle tests that break on every refactor
slides.markdown:
A **brittle test** fails when the production code's internal shape changes even though its external behavior didn't. This is the direct symptom of testing implementation instead of behavior (§6), and it's one of the most common reasons teams grow to resent their own test suite.

A telltale sign: you rename a private helper method or reorder two internal steps that don't change the output, run the suite, and five unrelated tests turn red. Now every refactor comes with an unplanned tax of "fix the tests," and eventually people stop refactoring at all, or start updating tests without reading why they failed — which quietly erases the tests' actual value.

The fix is the same principle stated as prevention: assert on inputs and outputs a caller would observe, use the public API to set up state, and resist the urge to verify *how* a result was computed unless that mechanism is itself the contract (e.g., "this must use a cache").

**Assertion roulette** is a single test asserting five unrelated things, so when it fails you're gambling on which assertion actually caused it:

```python
def test_process_order():
    order = process(cart)
    assert order.total == 42.50
    assert order.status == "confirmed"
    assert order.items[0].sku == "ABC123"
    assert len(inventory.reserved) == 1
    assert email_service.sent_count == 1
```

Most test frameworks stop at the first failing assertion, so you see "assert order.total == 42.50 failed" and have no idea whether the other four also would have failed — you fix the total, rerun, and discover a second failure you didn't know existed. That's a slow, serial discovery process for something a well-split test suite would have shown you all at once.

The fix is splitting: one test per behavior, so a red build immediately names the specific thing that broke, matching the "one reason to fail" principle this whole topic opened with.

These principles reinforce each other rather than standing alone. A test that follows AAA is naturally easier to keep to one behavior. A test that's isolated and fast (FIRST) is one people actually run before committing. A test named well is one where a violation of "one reason to fail" becomes obvious immediately, because the name promises one thing and the assertions deliver several.

In a real codebase you'll break one of these occasionally under time pressure — that's fine as a conscious trade-off. What separates a healthy suite from an eroding one is whether the team notices the trade-off and pays it back, or lets brittle, slow, multi-assert tests accumulate until nobody trusts red builds anymore.

Everything here assumed you could set up a unit's state cleanly and call it in isolation. Real code rarely cooperates — it depends on databases, clocks, other services, or objects that are slow or non-deterministic. The next topic, **Test Doubles & Mocking**, is about exactly that problem: how you isolate a unit from those dependencies without losing the behavior-not-implementation discipline you just built here.

Get that wrong — over-mock, or assert on internal call sequences instead of outcomes — and you reintroduce brittleness through the back door, coupling tests to implementation via the mock setup instead of via the production code directly.
